title: Why a carton of eggs is a luxury in Gaza
gist: A Sourcebase investigation finds that Israel's tightly controlled import system, with roughly eight approved traders selling truck space for coordination fees, plus border closures and smuggling, keeps eggs and fresh food in Gaza at two to four times prewar prices despite the ceasefire; Israel blames Hamas taxation, which traders dispute.

insights.claim: Before the war a 30-egg carton in Gaza cost about 14 shekels; in early October 2026 imported eggs ranged from 27 to 60 shekels, roughly two to four times prewar prices.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Food inflation in Gaza remains structural despite improved availability.
insights.locator: From staple to luxuryBefore the war

insights.claim: In summer 2025 famine conditions, eggs cost up to 600 shekels when they could be found.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Shows the extreme price sensitivity of Gaza to supply restrictions.

insights.claim: Tomatoes, once locally grown at 2-4 shekels per kg, peaked at 110 shekels per kg in northern Gaza last August per WFP monitoring, and are now bought in Israel at 1.5-2 shekels and wholesaled in Gaza for 7-8 shekels after coordination fees.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Quantifies the markup the import system adds to staples.
insights.locator: Tomatoes, for example, used to be locally grown

insights.claim: Food is more available than during the famine 14 months ago, but nutritious food remains economically out of reach for most residents.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Availability metrics overstate food security; affordability is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: the small supply of “nutritious food can be out of reach economically.”

insights.claim: Though there is a ceasefire, egg and other scarce-goods prices are unlikely to decline and could easily climb because Israel controls all crossings.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Do not expect ceasefire-driven normalization of Gaza's economy.
insights.quote: the prices of eggs and other scarce goods are unlikely to decline and could easily climb
insights.locator: Though there’s a ceasefire in Gaza

insights.claim: Israel permits only a small number of Palestinian traders, about eight according to traders, to import via Israeli companies, in a system partly designed to deny Hamas revenue and keep Gaza on the brink.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: A concentrated licensing chokepoint creates rents and pricing power for a few intermediaries.

insights.claim: Approved traders sell space on their trucks to smaller traders who pay tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars per shipment in coordination fees, which Palestinians call the 'coordination mafia'.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Coordination fees are the main driver of Gaza's food price premium.
insights.quote: pay tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars per shipment in what’s known as coordination fees
insights.locator: Palestinians refer to the Israeli trade restrictions

insights.claim: Trader Hussam Huwaiti buys eggs from an Israeli farmer at 13-15 shekels per carton, but coordination fees effectively double the price, and he sells at about 30 shekels to wholesalers.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Coordination fees roughly double landed cost per unit.

insights.claim: Huwaiti reports paying between 30,000 and 100,000 shekels per shipment in coordination fees, with no fixed fees, deals by phone and no paper trail.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Opaque, unrecorded fee markets invite corruption and profiteering.
insights.quote: “It’s a market, so there are no fixed fees,”
insights.locator: Huwaiti said he didn’t work with a specific coordinator

insights.claim: Coordination fees fall when crossings are open and rise with Israeli closures, such as for Jewish holidays and the Oct. 7 anniversary.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Crossing status is a leading indicator for Gaza food prices.
insights.quote: “When the crossings are open, the prices go down.”

insights.claim: Costs accrue at every leg: Ashdod customs duties, transport via an Israeli company, scanning fees at warehouses and checkpoints, and a fee to move goods across Kerem Shalom.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Layered fees make the supply chain structurally expensive.
insights.locator: Sometimes he works directly with the coordinator

insights.claim: Approved importer Mohammed Barqi says he charges no coordination fees but adds 12-13% profit for friends importing through him; one trader said he paid coordination fees to Barqi.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Competing accounts highlight the lack of transparency in the licensed trade.

insights.claim: Barqi bought eggs from Israeli supermarket chain Hatzi Hinam at 12 shekels a carton; a Kerem Shalom closure cost him 8,000 shekels per truck, total import cost was 168,000 shekels plus a 20,000-shekel profit.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Shows how delay costs at a single crossing compound into retail prices.
insights.locator: Barqi spoke to Sourcebase on Oct. 8

insights.claim: Cross-border smuggling rings involving Israeli soldiers, officials and businessmen are a major conduit for goods like cigarettes, medicines, solar panels and spare parts, pushing up prices.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Dual-use restrictions sustain a black market that inflates prices further.

themes.theme: Disputed blame and aid vs. commerce

insights.claim: A COGAT official said Israel is not responsible for Gaza prices and blamed Hamas taxes reaching up to 50%, while traders said Hamas did not tax or taxed inconsistently and basic food was not taxed.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Competing narratives on price causation matter for ICJ case and donor policy.
insights.locator: An official with the Coordinator of Government Activities

insights.claim: When Israel briefly cut commercial trade after Hamas proposed new fees, egg prices doubled in parts of Gaza.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Illustrates how sensitive Gaza prices are to any trade interruption.
insights.locator: For a few days this month

insights.claim: In the first two weeks of September, commercial trucks outnumbered aid trucks 1,765 to 693, about seven in ten, the highest commercial share recorded during the war per the Gaza Chamber of Commerce; COGAT says about half of roughly 600 daily trucks carry aid.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Gaza is shifting from aid to a paid commercial supply model that most residents cannot afford.

insights.claim: WFP recently cut the number of people receiving food aid in Gaza by 500,000, alongside cuts to cash assistance and hot meals, amid donor fatigue.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Aid funding shortfalls increase reliance on the costly commercial channel.

insights.claim: Israel imposed new NGO registration rules limiting which organizations can bring aid into Gaza, and key far-right ministers push to end assistance entirely.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Policy risk of further aid contraction.

insights.claim: Aid groups generally do not bring in eggs or fresh produce due to Israeli regulations and border delays, so nutritionally vital foods depend on the profit-driven import market.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Nutrition outcomes hinge on commercial trade rules, not aid volume.
insights.locator: Given Israeli regulations and unpredictable delays

insights.claim: UNCTAD says Gaza faces the world's worst economic crisis on record, with 92% of economic establishments damaged or destroyed and less than 1.5% of cropland accessible and undamaged.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
entities: UN Conference on Trade and Development
insights.so_what: Local production capacity is gone, making Gaza fully import-dependent.
insights.quote: 92% of economic establishments had been damaged or destroyed

insights.claim: Most of Gaza's 2.2 million people rely on international aid, and most remain displaced in the 30% of the territory not controlled by Israeli forces.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Reconstruction and normalization remain distant.

insights.claim: A cookie seller earning 22-24 shekels a day can afford bread and pasta but not eggs or meat, illustrating how incomes cannot meet current prices.
insights.speaker: Miriam Berger
insights.so_what: Purchasing power collapse is the core humanitarian driver.
insights.locator: This story was originally published by Sourcebase News
